Exits in the UK
1
Welcome to the second edition 
of the Exits in the UK report from 
Beauhurst and Triple Point. In this 
report, we look back at the past 
decade and the exits achieved by 
high-growth UK companies.  
 
The past decade has been a 
milestone decade for high-growth 
exits in the UK. During this time, UK 
and European start-up ecosystems 
have matured, attracting new 
and established venture capital 
investors seeking to support the 
ecosystem, and the promising 
startups within it. 
 
Today, these investors fund 
businesses at a rate incomparable 
to 10 years ago. As a result of this 
funding, more companies graduate 
to become attractive IPO candidates 
or acquisition targets. We are now 
seeing a significant increase in 
the number of successful exits, as 
these UK companies reach critical 
mass and sale, or IPO opportunities 
crystalise. 
 
Against this backdrop, we’ve 
prepared this report to shine a light 
on the state of UK company exits. 
After all, only with a robust and 
attractive path to exit can founders 
and investors realise the value they 
have worked hard to build.  
 
If the past 10 years were a 
milestone decade, 2021 was a 
milestone year. Rebounding from 
a difficult 2020, the total value 
of high-growth company exits 
last year increased to £26.7bn, a 
5x increase on 2020, and a 2.4x 
increase on the 10-year average. 
 
The success of 2021 has received 
wide press coverage, particularly 
with the record number of IPOs 
taking place. IPO volume was up 
3x on the 10-year average, and 
featured IPOs from well-known 
businesses including Wise, 
Darktrace and Deliveroo. 
 
Alongside these record-breaking 
numbers, 2021 continued trends 
that have been established for 
some time. B2B company exits are 
consistently more numerous than 
B2C company exits, with 579 B2B 
companies successfully exiting in 
2021 versus 294 B2C companies. 
This is something that has remained 
true since 2011, when our data 
began. 
Exit valuations follow a similar 
trend, although with some nuance. 
The mean exit valuation for B2B 
companies in 2021 was almost 3x 
than the B2C company average 
(£302m vs £119m), but the median 
was similar – and in fact slightly 
higher for B2C – at £51m versus 
£41m. 
 
What this aggregated data hides 
is that B2C continues to be the 
realm of the material outlier, fitting 
comfortably within the venture 
capital “home run” narrative. B2B 
exits are more granular and, while 
there are many notable B2B exits, 
the overall B2B total is made up 
of numerous smaller, strategic 
acquisitions. 
 
Coming out of 2021, it is worth 
reminding ourselves about the 
paucity of private acquisition data. 
While IPO data is plentiful, many 
acquisitions are more secretive—
particularly when the sale value 
is below £20m. Since 2011, 82% 
of acquisitions did not share deal 
data in the public domain. Our data 
collection and analysis adjusts for 
this, but it is still notable that so 
many exits have no data. 
 
As 2022 progresses, the UK start 
up ecosystem has much to be 
optimistic about, but there are 
clouds on the horizon. Early stage 
startup funding continues apace, 
and the number of mature, highly 
valued, later stage companies 
continues to grow. However 
stock market turmoil and macro-
economic challenges, such as 
inflation, represent obstacles that 
founders and their investors have 
to work hard to avoid. So far, the 
ecosystem has proved resilient – 
long may it continue.
 
Enjoy the report,
 
Seb Wallace
Seb Wallace,
VC Investor at 
Triple Point
“Only with a robust and 
attractive path to exit can 
founders and investors 
realise the value they have 
worked hard to build.”

Exits in the UK
2
As the number of companies 
Beauhurst has tracked has 
increased since we started in 2010, 
we naturally expected the number 
of exits to continue to grow. We did 
not expect, however, the impact 
that the pandemic would have on 
the number of exits in 2020, nor the 
rapid recovery that would take 
place in 2021. 
 
Exits are important to the UK’s high-
growth economy for three main 
reasons: the liquidity they provide 
to early investors providing them 
with capital back (and hopefully a 
gain) which can be re-invested into 
earlier stage startups; the release 
of the founders to start or back 
new ventures (though this doesn’t 
happen in every deal); and the 
platform for further expansion that 
an exit often provides.  
 
UK businesses are often criticised 
for exiting too early (particularly to 
foreign acquirers). But exits at an 
any stage create opportunities: the 
wealth they can create often gets 
recycled back into startups and 
scaleups; acquirers can elevate the 
commercialisation prospects of IP; 
the investment that comes with an 
acquisition or IPO creates jobs. It’s 
one thing to lament the lack of tech 
behemoths in the UK; it’s another 
to castigate founders and CEOs for 
pursuing exits. 
 
This report explores the UK exits 
that have taken place since 2011. 
Hopefully this report will prove both 
inspiring and useful to entrepreneurs 
and investors thinking about 
transactions of this sort.
Henry Whorwood,
Head of Research 
and Consultancy at 
Beauhurst

3
Methodology
Acquisitions 
 
 
An acquisition occurs when a 
company sells a majority (>50%) 
of its existing shares to another 
company or a fund. 
 
 
Initial public offerings 
(IPOs) 
An initial public offering occurs when 
the shares of a private company are 
first listed on a stock exchange. 
Industry acquisitions/trade 
sale
A trade sale occurs when a 
company’s shares are acquired by 
another company. Acquirers often 
seek to make use of an acquired 
company’s intellectual property, 
claim their market share, or to use 
the acquisition in a new market 
altogether. Trade sales make up 
the majority of acquisitions of high-
growth companies in the UK.
Fund acquisition/financial 
sale
Financial sales occur when the 
majority of a company’s shares are 
bought by a fund, usually private 
equity funds. Financial sales do occur 
in the high-growth space, but private 
equity firms tend to purchase later-
stage, established companies that 
are delivering consistent profit. 
 
 
Business-to-business (B2B) 
companies
B2B companies are companies that 
sell to other businesses. ‘Businesses’ 
refers to incorporated businesses 
(such as limited companies) as well 
as unincorporated businesses (such 
as partnerships or sole traders). A 
business can be a for-profit or a not-
for-profit enterprise.
Business-to-consumer (B2C) 
companies
B2C companies sell to consumers. 
‘Consumers’ refers to individuals 
who are engaging with a company 
on a personal basis, not in their 
capacity as employees or directors 
of a company or another entity. 
Companies can be both B2B and B2C. 
Beauhurst identifies ambitious businesses using eight triggers (outlined 
at the bottom of this page) that we believe suggests a company has 
high-growth potential. More detail on Beauhurst’s tracking triggers is 
available via our website.  
 
Equity investment 
To be included in our analysis, any investment must be:
• 
Some form of equity investment
• 
Secured by a non-listed UK company
• 
Issued between 1 January 2011 and 31 December 2021
 
Announced and unannounced fundraisings 
An unannounced fundraising is an investment made into a private 
company that is completed without press coverage or a statement 
from the recipient company or funds that made the investment. These 
transactions are an integral part of the UK’s high-growth economy, 
accounting for around 70% of all equity transactions.

Exits in the UK

Exits over time 
and types of exit
Between 2011 and 2021 there was a significant 
increase in both the number and value of exits 
completed by UK high-growth companies. 
The compound annual growth rate for the 
combined value of exits was 55.2% across 
these 10 years, reflecting the health of the 
UK’s high-growth economy. Unsurprisingly, 
exit figures experienced some turbulence 
during 2019 and 2020—caused by the 
COVID-19 pandemic and ongoing economic 
uncertainties due to the UK’s departure 
from the European Union. Despite the total 
value of exits plummeting by 70% to £5.1b in 
2019, marking a five-year low, the total value 
rebounded by the end of 2021—increasing by 
423% to £26.7b. As detailed on the following 
pages, both acquisitions and IPOs saw a 
dramatic uptick in 2021.

Exits in the UK
6
A total of 3,725 high-growth 
businesses exited via acquisition 
between 2011 and 2021, making it 
the dominant exit strategy for these 
UK companies. With the exception 
of 2020, a year where lockdowns 
impacted deal-making at all ticket 
sizes, there has been a clear positive 
trend in the number of companies 
acquired—rising from 23 in 2011 
to 732 in 2021. This trend is less 
notable when observing the value 
of acquisitions, which has varied 
considerably.
The cause of these fluctuations is 
partially due to the limited valuation 
data available for the majority of 
deals. For 82% of acquisitions, no 
deal data is available in the public 
domain. Moreover, the data can also 
become skewed by when large, 
announced acquisitions do appear, 
as they contribute significantly 
towards annual totals. For example, 
when Skyscanner was acquired by 
Ctrip International for £1.4b in 2016, 
this accounted for 18% of the total 
acquisition value that year.  Looking 
at recent trends, data for 2021 points 
towards a promising future. The total 
quantity of deals increased by 66.4% 
from 440 in 2020 to 732 in 2021 as 
the UK economy began to open up.

Exits in the UK
7
For both trade and financial sales, 
growth trends mimic those of the 
broader acquisition category. Both 
trade and fund sales became steadily 
more numerous during the 10-year 
period, and neither escaped a dip in 
popularity during 2020. Since 2011, 
the ratio between these two forms of 
acquisition has remained relatively 
stable, with trade sales representing 
85-90% of transactions. 
An acquisition falls into the category 
of a trade sale where the company 
acquired is purchased by another 
company. This exit strategy is popular 
when the acquiring company hopes 
to use the intellectual property of 
the acquired company, or claim their 
market share. An example of a trade 
sale with the latter purpose is the 
acquisition of online on-demand 
supermarket delivery service Weezy by 
competitor Getir in November 2021. 
Fund sales, on the other hand, are led 
by funds that acquire companies at a 
later, more established stage. These 
buyers are often looking to increase a 
company’s revenue or profits through 
a change in management and/or 
strategy, with a view to subsequently 
exiting the company again via another 
acquisition or IPO. One example of this 
is the 2013 acquisition of Dr Martens 
by the fund Permira Credit Solutions, 
a transaction that was followed by an 
IPO in January 2021.

Exits in the UK
8
For exits completed by UK high- 
growth companies, listing is 
less popular than undergoing an 
acquisition —only 10.1% of exits 
in 2021 were IPOs. However, the 
number of businesses listing has 
increased by a compound annual 
growth rate of 25% between 2012 
and 2021. Similar to acquisitions, 
the total value of companies 
undertaking an IPO fluctuates 
when those companies that list 
in a given year secure very large 
market capitalisations. This is best 
evidenced by the IPO of medical 
instrument provider Convatec
in 2016. The company listed at a 
valuation of £4.4b, making up 55% 
of the total figure for high-growth 
companies undertaking an IPO in 
that year.
In parallel to the broader economic 
instability of 2019 and 2020, both 
the number and value of IPOs 
decreased significantly
as a result of pandemic-related 
insecurities. But both figures 
rebounded and then grew in 2021 
when a record number of high-
growth companies (49) floated, 
securing a combined market 
capitalisation of £20.6b, reflecting 
not a recovery in financial markets 
but also increased appetites 
for listing. The companies that 
undertook an IPO in 2021 included 
life sciences businesses Exscientia 
and Immunocore, valued at £4.8b 
and £1.7b respectively.

Exits in the UK
9
For high-growth company exits 
between 2011 and 2021, the number 
of B2B businesses that participated 
in either an acquisition or IPO is 
more than double that of B2C 
companies. Although in 2011 the 
number of exits in both categories 
was below 20, by 2021, the number 
of B2B exits had climbed to 579 
while the count of B2C exits stood 
at 284. 
Exits by companies targeting other 
businesses increased by over 30 
times in the last decade, with 12 of 
these deals valued at over £1b. One 
of the largest deals in this category 
was secured by Markit, a financial 
data provider, when it underwent 
an IPO in June 2014  with a market 
capitalisation of £2.53b. Another 
highly valued B2B exit took place 
in 2018, when FNZ—a developer 
of wealth management and 
investment platforms, was acquired 
by CDPQ-Generation Partnership 
for £1.65b. 
The number of exits by companies 
focused on consumers experienced 
more modest growth in the same 
period. This is most likely the result 
of a larger proportion of the high-
growth population working with a 
B2B model. Among high-growth 
companies, 66.3% are categorised 
as B2B, whilst only 45.3% of 
businesses have a B2C focus.

B2B versus B2C: 
exit valuations
Although mean valuations for both business 
models fluctuate to a certain extent, the 
average value of B2C exits has varied 
significantly over the last decade. In 2012 this 
figure was lowest when the mean exit valuation 
for B2C companies was a mere £19.6m. Just 
two years later, this number peaked at £311m. 
These changes are more evident for B2C 
businesses than B2B companies, because the 
B2C industry is more competitive, and only 
a few companies capture the market share. 
When one of these successful businesses exits, 
it causes the average in that year to become 
inflated. The difference between the median 
valuations for B2B and B2C companies shows 
this. For companies working with a B2B model, 
the median valuation has remained relatively 
constant, as more companies share the market. 
In comparison, when looking at B2C companies 
there is a greater degree of change in the 
average valuation received each year.

Exits in the UK
11
Exit case studies
These companies exited from the high-growth 
ecosystem of the UK between 2021 and 2022. 
Each nation in the UK is represented, along 
with both exit types: IPO and acquisition. 
These companies span a range of sectors, 
showcasing the variety of high-value 
businesses exiting in the UK. Exscientia and 
TC BioPharm are both companies working 
within the life sciences industry, whereas 
Repstor works in data management and 
Vortex IOT develops a product for the risk 
management sector. Each of these businesses 
benefited from equity investment prior to exit, 
showcasing the power of funding as a tool 
for maximising growth in private companies. 
Notably, the leaders and backers of the more 
capital-intensive life sciences companies opted 
to pursue IPOs rather than acquisitions. Public 
markets perform an important role in providing 
ongoing financing for capital intensive and 
speculative undertakings like drug discovery.
Exscientia
Date of exit  
 
 
01/10/2021
Type of exit 
 
 
IPO 
 
University of Dundee spinout Excientia secured £300m of equity investment 
across seven fundraising rounds prior to floating in October 2021. The business 
develops an artificial intelligence drug discovery platform that designs and 
tests millions of small molecule drugs to understand which of these will make 
successful drugs.
Repstor
Date of exit 
 
 
23/06/2021
Type of exit   
 
 
Acquisition
 
Launched in February 2012, Repstor developed a software assisting public 
and private organisations to gather, manage and archive press-related 
documentation. Prior to its acquisition in 2021, the company secured £564k of 
equity investment across four fundraising rounds. 
TC BioPharm
Date of exit  
 
 
11/02/2022
Type of exit   
 
 
IPO
Prior to floating in February 2022, TC BioPharm raised £22.2m of equity 
investment and £11.7m of grant funding, in support of their development of 
pharmaceuticals to combat cancer. The company aims to create safe, cost-
effective cell therapies, with their leading product—OmnImmune—in late-stage 
clinical trials for the treatment of blood cancer. 
Vortex IoT
Date of exit  
 
 
18/01/2022
Type of exit   
 
 
Acquisition
Vortex IoT designs wireless sensor networks that are used in harsh 
environments to collect data which can be monitored remotely and assessed for 
risk. Targeting both the heavy industry and infrastructure sectors, the company 
has secured £2.26m of equity investment and £1.56m of grant funding.

For the 855 exits by high-growth companies 
which have valuation data available, 18.5 % of 
these businesses were valued below £50m 
whilst 8.19% of companies exited with a 
valuation below £10m. Both of these brackets 
were populated with essentially an even 
number of IPOs and acquisitions—although 
it should be noted that there is proportionally 
more data available for IPOs than acquisitions. 
The valuation brackets for exits worth more 
than £500m are almost exclusively occupied 
by IPOs (83%), with 11 businesses securing a 
market capitalisation above £1b. The purchase 
of professional service provider Turner & 
Townsend by the American firm CBRE in 
November 2021 was the only acquisition with 
a valuation above £1b.

Exits in the UK
14
Since 2011, mean exit valuations for 
high-growth companies undertaking 
an IPO have been volatile. These 
figures have the capacity to fluctuate 
by over 100% each year, mostly 
caused by individual high-value exits 
that inflate annual statistics. Despite 
this turbulence, there has been 
an overall growth in the average 
value of IPOs during this 10-year 
period, caused by an unprecedented 
amount of capital available to private 
companies prior to going public. 
At the beginning of the same 
decade, exit valuations for acquired 
companies had less annual variation 
and a more modest growth trajectory. 
However, over the past three 
years, this figure has experienced 
a similar degree of turbulence as 
that observed for IPOs—most likely 
influenced by macroeconomic 
factors such as Brexit and the 
COVID-19 pandemic, including the 
associated economic stimulus. 
This turbulence has also been 
accompanied by a significant 
increase in the mean exit valuation 
for acquisitions. Prior to 2018, this 
number peaked at £107m in 2015, 
as acquisition values remained 
distinctly lower than those achieved 
by companies that underwent an IPO. 
However, in 2019 the mean valuation 
for companies that were acquired 
shot to £282m, and subsequently 
peaked in 2021 at £364m.

15
The relative stability of the upper 
quartile of exit valuations for businesses 
that have undergone an IPO, in 
comparison to the same mean exit 
valuations, showcases the impact of a 
handful of market capitalisations. With 
the exception of a peak in 2014, the 
upper quartile of IPO exit valuations 
have remained constant, with the 
exclusion of very large deals pointing 
towards an underlying consistency in 
these valuations. A similar conclusion 
can be drawn when analysing the 
lower quartile of IPO exit valuations, 
which have displayed the same 
consistency across the 10-year period. 
The quartile data for acquisitions has 
evidenced a degree of consistency 
between 2011 and 2021, which is 
largely to be expected as the mean 
exit valuations for these companies 
have, for the most part, avoided 
dramatic fluctuations. Nevertheless, it 
is interesting to note the differences 
between 2019 and 2021. As noted 
previously, the mean exit valuations 
increased dramatically in 2019, an 
experience that carried across the 
range of valuation quartiles. A similar 
peak in mean exit valuations occured 
in 2021, however, this did not follow 
through into the various quartiles. 
This data suggests that in 2019 the 
increase in mean valuations took 
place as a result of a large volume of 
higher-value transactions, whereas in 
2021, the growth was caused by a few 
high-value acquisitions.

Exits in the UK
16
Among the 3,730 high-growth 
companies that have been acquired 
since 2011, a number of valuable 
transactions were secured: 22 
companies were acquired at a price 
above £500m, with seven of these 
businesses being purchased for 
over £1b. The largest of these was 
for Yorkshire-based Firth Rixson, 
which was acquired by the American 
firm Alcoa in 2014, for the purpose 
of expanding its market leadership. 
Urbanest, a provider of university 
accommodation, underwent the 
second most valuable acquisition 
amongst high-growth businesses 
in 2020, when the company was 
purchased by Scape Group for £1.75b. 
The businesses acquired for over £1b 
operate within a range of sectors, 
spanning across human resources, 
marketing, and data aggregation. 
Synergy, a high-growth company 
that was acquired for £1.24b by 
McCann Worldgroup in 2020, provides 
services to businesses centred around 
increasing employee engagement.
Moreover, despite the London-centric 
nature of the UKs broader high-growth 
ecosystem, only two of these seven 
businesses were headquartered 
in the capital at the time of their 
exit: FNZ and Urbanest. Two were 
headquartered in each of the regions 
of the South East and Yorkshire and 
the Humberside, whilst SkyScanner 
was Scotland-based.

Exits in the UK

UK high-growth companies that IPO 
tend to achieve far higher valuations 
at exit than those received by 
acquired companies. Many of the top 
companies by value floating on public 
markets had market capitalisations 
several times higher than acquired 
counterparts. The IPO undertaken 
by Wise, the largest of any high-
growth company in the UK, received a 
market capitalisation of £7.69b—four 
times more than the most valuable 
acquisition. 
Following Wise in the ranking, 
e-commerce specialists The Hut 
Group and FarFetch floated at £4.85b 
and £4.44b respectively. Prior to 
listing, both companies secured 
equity funding to support the projects 
such as international expansion and 
brand development. Across 12 funding 
rounds, the Hut Group benefited 
from £476m of equity investment. 
Similarly, FarFetch received £516m of 
equity funding across nine rounds.  
Another sector represented widely in 
the ranking is life sciences. Working 
in this sector is Oxford Nanopore 
Technologies, a company widely known 
for its production of rapid COVID-19 
tests and DNA sequencing devices, 
which underwent an IPO with a market 
capitalisation of £3.38b. Other life 
sciences firms securing large market 
capitalistions include Convatec 
(£4.39b) and Exscientia (£2.37b).
